The facility’s feed shed currently contains at least three bags of primate food that expired on July 9, 2026. These bags of
feed are intended for consumption by the facility’s two adult black-and-white ruffed lemurs.
Expired food can have decreased nutritive value and palatability, which can be detrimental to the health of the animals
that consume it. Any food fed by the facility must be clean, wholesome, and palatable to the animals. It must be of
sufficient quantity and have sufficient nutritive value to maintain a healthful condition and weight range of the animals and
to meet its normal daily nutritional requirements.
To be corrected by July 30, 2026.

The licensee did not maintain an enclosure housing one 4-month-old female capybara in good repair to contain the
animal, which resulted in the animal’s death. According to facility records, the facility received the young capybara on April
27, 2026. A facility representative stated that they had not expected to receive the animal and did not have a specific
enclosure prepared for her, so they placed her in the kangaroo enclosure adjacent to the enclosure housing two adult
capybaras. These two enclosures share a fenceline that has a chained metal gate connecting them. The facility
representative stated that there was a wooden board attached at the base of the fence posts on the kangaroo side which
blocked the gap beneath the gate; however, this wooden board was not present at the time of inspection.
According to the facility representatives, on April 30, 2026, animal caretakers found the young capybara deceased in the
enclosure of the adult capybaras. The facility believed that the animal fit between the wooden board and the base of the
gate in order to get into the other enclosure. During the inspection, the inspector measured the distance between the
bottom of the gate and the ground and found a gap that ranged from 5 to 7 inches along the length. When the inspector
asked how the gate was usually chained, the facility representative showed the inspector multiple ways, some of which
resulted in a gap between where the wooden board would have been and the bottom of the gate. This gap was large
enough for the young capybara to get through.
Enclosures with gates that do not close securely and leave gaps large enough for a young animal to fit through are not in
good repair and can lead to escape, injury, or death. The facility must be constructed of such material and such strength
as appropriate for the animals involved. The indoor and outdoor housing facilities shall be maintained in good repair to
protect the animals from injury and to contain the animals.
To be corrected from this day, July 24, 2026, forward.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with facility representatives.
